title: Reading the Crust
passage:
There are three hundred and forty pans on the Aveste flats, each about the size of a tennis court, floored with grey clay that is trodden flat again every spring. Sea water enters the chain at the north end in March and takes eleven weeks to reach the last pond, losing four fifths of itself on the way. What is left is raked out with a wooden lath, dried in open sheds and sold unwashed. Two hundred and twelve of the pans belong to the cooperative that registered the Aveste mark in 2014; the rest are worked by two families who never joined and sell under no name at all. The mark is precise about equipment. It names the lath, keeps metal out of the pan, bars washing and heat-drying, and sets out how the sheds are ventilated. Salt that carries it fetches about six times the price of the bagged industrial grade.

Iria Solbes has spent five seasons on the flats trying to establish which of those rules is doing the work. She is a brine chemist with a laboratory in the old customs house and a standing arrangement with eleven pan-holders, and her method is unglamorous: take salt from one pond under two conditions and put both before a panel that is never told which is which. Over five seasons the panels separated nothing the mark regulates. Lath-raked salt and salt lifted with a plastic scoop came out level, and so did clay against the three pans relined with concrete in 2019. What the panels did separate, in every season and by a wide margin, was dwell — the number of days the brine had stood in the final pond before the salt was taken off it. Salt lifted at three days carried roughly a fifth less magnesium than salt from the same pond lifted at eight, the bittern having had that much longer to concentrate. "A panel tells you what a mouth can find, and a mouth is not a stable instrument," Solbes says. "But that one came back five times, and the rules we protect never came back at all."

None of which is an argument against the lath, and Solbes is careful to say so. Dwell can be got right at Aveste because a lath and a plank can be carried out at any hour of any day, by one person, at an hour's notice. The saltern at Pella Marsa, forty kilometres up the coast, was floored in the 1990s to take a small harvester, and its dates are settled before the season opens, because the contractor who owns the machine works six sites between March and September. The brine there stands as long as the calendar says it stands. Solbes's panels can pick Pella Marsa out of a line-up too, and it is not that the harvester bruises the crystal. It is that the harvester comes on a Tuesday. The mark protects the lath. What the lath protects is the morning.

Teodor Panek, who chairs the certifying body, has read all of it and disputes none of it. His objection is procedural. "You can photograph a lath," he says. "You cannot photograph a decision about whether the crust is ready." A mark, on his account, is an instrument against fraud rather than a description of a craft, and it has to hold up for an inspector who arrives unannounced and is gone the same afternoon. Solbes agrees with every word of that and has said so in print. Then she points to the concrete. On chemistry the three relined pans behave like the clay ones. But concrete dries faster at the edges, and the pair who worked those pans in 2019 and 2020 misread the crust in both seasons and lifted late; by 2021 they had the new floors by heart and the lateness stopped. Nothing in the salt recorded the relining. The people did.

Solbes has asked for one more line on the certificate, a dwell window of three to five days in the final pond, and has not got it. The committee has not refused it either. It has asked how an inspector arriving on a Thursday is to verify a number that was only true on Tuesday morning, and nobody has answered that yet. So the mark goes on guaranteeing a wooden lath, which no panel in five seasons has managed to taste, while the pan-holders go on standing at the last pond at six in the morning working out whether today is the day, which every panel can taste, and nothing at Aveste writes that part down.
— Hedda Marston

saltern = a chain of shallow ponds in which sea water is evaporated to salt
bittern = the bitter liquor left when sea water has given up most of its salt

questions.prompt: What are we told about the Aveste mark?

options.text: It governs every pan on the flats, which is what allows the name to command its price.
The cooperative has never set down in writing which of its methods the name actually requires of members.
It was registered to stop producers on neighbouring coasts from selling their salt under the Aveste name.
Registered in 2014, it fixes the equipment and forbids washing, and covers about two thirds of the pans.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-001 (direct detail retrieval), anchored in paragraph 1. WHY-KEY (D): three separate statements combine into it — "the cooperative that registered the Aveste mark in 2014"; "The mark is precise about equipment. It names the lath, keeps metal out of the pan, bars washing and heat-drying, and sets out how the sheds are ventilated"; and "Two hundred and twelve of the pans" out of "three hundred and forty", which is about two thirds. The key recasts all three in different words rather than lifting any run of them. It is deliberately the flat, confident, counted option: on this question the cautious-sounding choice (B) is wrong, so a solver who reaches for the hedged answer scores nothing. WHY-NOT-A (trap: quantifier_upgrade): a registered mark that fetches six times the industrial price reads as though it must cover the place it is named after, and the passage never labels any salt as unmarked in so many words. It fails on the count — 212 of 340 pans are in the cooperative, and "the rest are worked by two families who never joined and sell under no name at all". WHY-NOT-B (trap: over-hedged contradiction): written as the measured, plausible-sounding wrong answer, since craft marks often are vague about method. The passage states the opposite in a short verdict sentence — "The mark is precise about equipment" — and then lists four things it specifies. WHY-NOT-C (trap: outside_knowledge): protecting a place name against imitators elsewhere on the same coast is the ordinary real-world purpose of a registration of this kind, so a passage-blind reader has no ground to reject it. The text gives no reason for the registration at all; it only reports what the mark contains and what the salt sells for.

questions.prompt: What does the text say about the saltern at Pella Marsa?

options.text: Its floors were laid to take a machine, and its harvest dates are settled ahead of the season.
Its salt was told apart from Aveste's in every trial because the harvester damages the crystals as it lifts them.
It is worked by two families who stayed outside the cooperative and sell their salt under no protected name.
Its output is washed and graded before sale, which is what separates it from the salt raked at Aveste.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-001 (direct detail retrieval), anchored in paragraph 3. WHY-KEY (A): "The saltern at Pella Marsa … was floored in the 1990s to take a small harvester, and its dates are settled before the season opens, because the contractor who owns the machine works six sites between March and September." The option paraphrases the floor and the fixed calendar without reusing a distinctive run. Like the key at q1 it is specific and unhedged, which keeps "correct" and "qualified" from lining up across the unit. WHY-NOT-B (trap: half-right conjunction with a mechanism the text explicitly refuses): the first half is nearly true — "Solbes's panels can pick Pella Marsa out of a line-up too" — and mechanical damage to crystals is the intuitive reason a machine-harvested salt would taste different. The passage rules the mechanism out in the next clause: "it is not that the harvester bruises the crystal. It is that the harvester comes on a Tuesday." "Every trial" also upgrades what is said. WHY-NOT-C (trap: wrong_location): every element is true one paragraph away, of Aveste, where "the rest are worked by two families who never joined and sell under no name at all". A reader who remembers two families and an unprotected salt attaches them to the wrong saltern. WHY-NOT-D (trap: outside_knowledge): washing and grading is what an industrially harvested salt would ordinarily undergo, and the passage does make a point of Aveste salt being "sold unwashed", which invites the contrast. Nothing is said about what happens to Pella Marsa's salt after it is lifted.

questions.prompt: What is implied about the three pans that were relined with concrete in 2019?

options.text: Since the salt came out the same either way, the choice of floor can now be made on cost alone.
The change showed up in how the pans had to be read, rather than in the salt that came off them.
The two late seasons leave it unclear whether pans floored in concrete can meet the mark at all.
Drying faster at the edges gave those pans a crust with more magnesium in it than the clay ones.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-002 (inference / implication), one logical inch beyond paragraph 4. The passage supplies the two halves and leaves the reader to put them together: "On chemistry the three relined pans behave like the clay ones. But concrete dries faster at the edges, and the pair who worked those pans in 2019 and 2020 misread the crust in both seasons and lifted late; by 2021 they had the new floors by heart and the lateness stopped." WHY-KEY (B): a floor that alters when the crust looks ready, without altering the salt, is a change in the reading task and nothing else — which is what the paragraph's closing pair of sentences asserts in another register. WHY-NOT-A (trap: too_far — a real premise carried one step past what the text supports): it takes the true chemistry finding and draws a purchasing rule from it, which the two misread seasons stand against; the passage's own point is that the relining cost something the salt never showed. WHY-NOT-C (trap: over-hedged non-sequitur): built to be the careful-sounding option, so that hedging is not a route to the key here. The mark as described governs the lath, metal, washing, drying and ventilation of sheds — not what a pan is floored with — and the lateness had stopped by 2021, so nothing is left unclear in the way the option claims. WHY-NOT-D (trap: surface_word_match): it recycles the passage's own "dries faster at the edges" and its magnesium figure into a claim the text denies, since the panels put the relined pans level with the clay ones. Faster drying at the rim also sounds like exactly the sort of thing that would concentrate a mineral, which is what makes it tempting.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's attitude to the objection Panek raises?

options.text: The writer adopts his position that a mark exists to stop fraud, and leaves the craft question there.
The writer treats it as cover for a committee that would rather not reopen rules it has already written.
The writer allows that the objection is a fair one, and still does not let it close the argument.
The writer finds it largely answered by Solbes, with only the inspector's unannounced visit left as a difficulty.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-005 (stance / attitude), anchored in paragraphs 4 and 5. WHY-KEY (C): the concession is unmistakable and is made in the text's own arrangement of the material — Panek "has read all of it and disputes none of it", his objection is called "procedural" rather than evasive, and Solbes "agrees with every word of that and has said so in print". Yet the piece does not stop there: it reports that the question of verification "nobody has answered … yet" and then closes on a sentence that sets the guaranteed lath, which no panel could taste, against the six-o'clock judgement at the last pond, which every panel could, and "nothing at Aveste writes that part down". Fair objection, argument still open. WHY-NOT-A (trap: role_or_attribution_swap — the TYPE-005 signature): the fraud-versus-craft framing is Panek's, given in his voice and in his quoted line about photographing a lath, and the writer reports it without visible resistance for a full paragraph. Handing it to the writer as a settled conclusion misses the final paragraph, which reopens exactly the question the framing would have closed. WHY-NOT-B (trap: polarity overshoot): dismissal is too strong for a text that calls the objection procedural and then records that "The committee has not refused it either" and that it put a real and unanswered question. Nothing in the piece suggests bad faith. WHY-NOT-D (trap: measured-sounding weight reversal): written to feel as balanced as the key, so that picking the moderate-sounding option decides nothing. It inverts the paragraph — Solbes does not answer Panek, she agrees with him — and the inspector's visit is not a residual difficulty but the whole obstacle that has kept the dwell window off the certificate.

questions.prompt: What is this text mainly about?

options.text: How one chemist's tasting panels overturned a coastal industry's faith in the value of its hand tools.
A protected method guards what an inspector can see, while the salt turns on a judgement nobody records.
That traditional saltmaking survives on its price premium and would not otherwise outlast mechanised production.
That machine harvesting spoils sea salt in ways a tasting panel can detect but chemistry cannot explain.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-004 (main idea / whole-text gist), edge position 5. WHY-KEY (B): the gap between what a certificate can hold and what actually makes the salt is the spine of the piece. Paragraph 1 is an inventory of what the mark specifies; paragraph 2 shows the panels separating none of it and separating dwell instead; paragraph 3 explains why the tools nonetheless matter, as the thing that leaves the timing free; paragraph 4 supplies the reason a mark is written that way, in Panek's line about photographing a decision; paragraph 5 closes on the lath that no panel could taste, the morning judgement that every panel could, and the fact that "nothing at Aveste writes that part down". The key states this flatly rather than in hedges, so the qualified-sounding options here (A's sweeping verb aside, C's conditional) are not the way in. WHY-NOT-A (trap: scope_error with an overstatement): the research is the most vivid thread in the piece and a solver who fixes on paragraph 2 will reach for it, but nothing was overturned — the mark still guarantees the lath, the committee has not moved, and Solbes herself says her results are "not an argument against the lath". WHY-NOT-C (trap: outside_knowledge): the six-times price is in the text, and an economic account of why handmade goods persist is the sort of thesis a piece like this often carries, which is what makes it hard to dismiss blind. The passage never argues about the survival of the trade, and never compares Aveste's economics with anyone's. WHY-NOT-D (trap: surface_word_match assembling a causal story out of the text's own terms): tasting panels, machine harvesting and chemistry are all the passage's vocabulary, and the panels really can pick Pella Marsa out. The text denies the mechanism outright — "it is not that the harvester bruises the crystal" — and its chemistry is not baffled but explanatory, since dwell shows up as magnesium.

generator_meta.topic: sea-salt harvesting and salterns — a protected craft mark that fixes the tools while the measurable quality turns on an unrecorded timing judgement
